A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIMO framework, and their text, equations and exhibits support reliable comparison. Neither contains an appendix. V2 references a separate supplement; its unavailable results are excluded from this assessment.

before.justification: V1 reports original generated-video examples demonstrating character, motion and scene control, particularly in Figures 5–7.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthesis examples, quantitative baseline comparisons and component ablations in Figures 5–8 and Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: The spatial decomposition, SMPL-anchored motion codes, canonical appearance transfer, scene/occlusion encoding, diffusion decoder and training objective are retained. Specifying 6,890 SMPL vertices adds implementation detail without establishing a changed method.

E1.justification: HUD-7K training data, AMASS/Mixamo motions, arbitrary-character animation and interactive real-world video scenarios remain. The new 100-clip evaluation formalizes testing within this existing coverage rather than introducing a distinct task or domain.

E2.justification: V1 cites animation methods but reports no direct baseline evaluation. V2 Figure 6 and Table 1 add qualitative and quantitative comparisons against Animate Anyone, Mimic-Motion and Champ, with reported fine-tuning on the authors' training data.

E3.justification: V2 introduces evaluation on 100 collected videos randomly truncated to 150-frame clips, using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and FVD, plus baseline fine-tuning. The reported training batch size also changes from 4 to 8, while approximately 50,000 iterations and 24-frame training clips remain; this does not establish whether earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Section 4.3 adds tests removing spatial decomposition, independent occlusion encoding and canonical appearance transfer, and replacing structured motion codes with 2D skeletons or 3D maps. Table 2 and Figures 7–8 provide quantitative and visual evidence; the occlusion-removal variant is shown qualitatively. V1 contains no corresponding component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's quantitative tables contain point estimates only.

E6.justification: V2 adds numerical results absent from v1. Table 1 reports MIMO at 25.210 PSNR, 0.883 SSIM, 0.125 LPIPS and 221.4 FVD, leading all three comparators on these metrics. Table 2 adds component results, including PSNR 22.148 without spatial decomposition. These are newly reported evaluations, not measured gains over v1 under matched settings.

T1.justification: The spatial masking equation and diffusion noise-prediction loss remain equivalent. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and specifying the existing SMPL representation's vertex count introduces no new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central claims about character, motion and scene control remain. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of outperforming prior methods by a large margin and recasts the existing controllable-synthesis task as a new task contribution; v1 already described video character replacement as an application.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands component-specific explanations: background distortions are attributed to absent scene guidance, limitations of 3D maps to undefined dense body-part labels, and reduced hand/foot confusion to canonical appearance transfer improving motion learning. These interpretations accompany new comparator and ablation evidence beyond v1's general architectural rationale.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies PyTorch, 80 GB GPU memory and 6,890 SMPL-anchored codes, and describes obtaining and fine-tuning comparator implementations. Initialization, frozen components and eight A100 GPUs were already documented. The project URL remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated Related Work section substantially expanding discussion of 3D human modeling and diffusion-based animation. Newly discussed works include NeuMan, HOSNeRF, AG3D and EVA3D, with fuller positioning around reconstruction costs, motion representation and human–scene interaction.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction and method prose is retained. V2 revises the abstract and contribution bullets, inserts Related Work before the method, groups implementation details, and converts the three numbered control subsections into paragraph headings. Much of the additional text documents new scientific comparisons rather than rewriting existing material.

P2.justification: The standalone diverse-character gallery in v1 Figure 5 is omitted, while selected motion and scene panels from v1 Figures 6–7 are condensed into v2 Figure 5. New baseline and ablation Figures 6–8 and Tables 1–2 substantially reorganize the experimental presentation.

improvement.justification: V1 relies on selected visual demonstrations without comparative or component validation. V2 substantially addresses this deficiency through a defined evaluation protocol, three-baseline comparisons and targeted ablations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 6–8. These additions make the central design choices considerably more assessable. The compressed character gallery and unavailable supplementary comparisons limit some evidence, but the main-text validation provides a clear substantial net improvement.
